In the aftermath of this event, a pamphlet circulated that denounced the "Four Traitors" who "sold themselves" to one faction of this conflict, including the corpulently depicted Samuel F. Man. A field hospital for one side in this conflict was at the Pettingill-Mason House. The leader of one side of this conflict fought against his uncle Crawford Allen, and his own father Sullivan. One side held the town of Woonsocket, while another held the People's Convention. One faction in this conflict elected Samuel Ward King as their leader, and a Supreme Court case about this event ruled that the conflict in question was a "political question" and thus not justiciable. Ruled upon in Luther v. Borden, name this rebellion that happened after two governors were elected in Rhode Island.

In the late 19th century, this country's politics saw the "Transformation Movement" in which Conservative members of Parliament supported Liberal prime ministers. In the 1920's, this country was home to a secessionist insurgent group called TIGR. The Acerbo Law reformed this country's parliament, and the Irishwoman Violet Gibson attempted to assassinate a Prime Minister of this country. Operation Oak was a German commando raid against a target in this country led by Otto Skorzeny during World War II. One period in this country's history is known as the "Salo Republic." During an unstable period known as the "Days of Lead," the Red Brigades kidnapped and killed this country's Prime Minister. During World War II, German defenses in this country included the Bernhardt and Hitler lines, which made up the Winter Line, the breaching of which was an objective in the battle of Monte Cassino. Name this country that has been led by Aldo Moro, Giuliano Amato, and Silvio Berlusconi.

One commander killed at this battle left a widow who married Duke Welf of Bavaria. Prior to this battle, the winners made camp at Tadcaster, while the losers made camp at Riccall and made a crossing of the Derwent River at Kexby. According to one account, that losing side, which was in league with King Malcolm III, had not brought their chainmail to this battle. A force under the command of Eystien Orre joined this battle in its final moments, but proved remarkably ineffective. This battle was preceded by one at the Gate of Fulford, which saw the defeat of Morcar of Northumbria and Edwin of Mercia. One person killed in this battle was succeeded by his sons Magnus and Olaf, while another fatality was the victor's brother Tostig. Name this battle where Harold Hardrada was defeated by Harold Godwinson, which took place mere days before Hastings.

Richard Call was the second territorial delegate from this future state, and served as its territorial governor twice; his nephew Wilkinson Call was a Civil War general and Senator from this state. The first statehood governor was William Moseley. This state saw a mass lynching known as the Rosewood Massacre. Civil War battles in this state include the Battle of Natural Bridge, the Battle of Marianna, and the Battle of Olustee. This state, which saw the 1980 Arthur McDuffie riots after an incident of police brutality, elected the first Jewish Senator, David Levy Yulee. Confederate Secretary of the Navy Stephen Mallory hailed from this state. An international incident during the Monroe administration occurred when Andrew Jackson served as its territorial governor; he had earlier entered this future state to capture and hang British subjects. The site of the Treaty of Payne's Landing and three same-named Indian Wars, name this home state of Osceola and Janet Reno, which decided the 2000 Presidential election.

Philip Khoury said that the Arab kind of this was a conservative tool of the urban landowners of Damascus to maintain their position, while Michael Provence asserted that it first became widespread among Syrian Druze communities. Michael Billig wrote about rituals during sporting events to discuss the "banal" kind of it, while Liah Greenfeld placed its origin in Tudor England among upwardly mobile commoners. Anthony Smith believed it was the outgrowth of ethnic kinship, while Ernest Gellner believed it was an inevitable byproduct of industrialization since people sought to make cultural and political units "congruent." Its rise required the exchange of information made possible by "print capitalism," which emphasized the common bonds uniting "imagined communities" according to the theories of Benedict Anderson. Originating in Europe only in the modern era, this is, what ideology that also gave its name to the political party of Chiang Kai-Shek?

According to Cosmas Indicopleustes, the ruler of this kingdom lived in a palace decorated by unicorn statues. A merchant guidebook called the Periplus of the Erythrean Sea describes this polity and its miserly ruler King Erythrean and says that its major port was Adulis. Justinian sent an ambassador named Julian to this kingdom, who reported that its ruler wore a loincloth of gold fiber. During the reigh of King Afilas, this kingdom defeated King Shammar Yuharish, and later this empire crushed the Himyarites, a sect of fanatical Jews. Frumentius, a Syrian monk, brought Christianity to this kingdom during the reign of King Ezana. At its height, this kingdom ruled Yemen and its northern neighbor, the Kingdom of Kush. Name this early Christian Ethiopian state.

In the leadup to this conflict, one side failed to renew the Bilateral Treaty on Immigration, in no small part due to anger over the increased presence of one side's shoemakers in the other's capital city. The National Conciliation Party won a victory in elections following this conflict after Fidel Sanchez Hernandez apologized for his role in it. The creation of FENAGH spurred on one side of this conflict, which saw one side's leader Oswaldo Lopez Arellano provided weapons by Anastacio Somoza. This conflict saw the last battle between propeller planes, and it was spurred when a political party was created by the United Fruit Company. Also known as the hundred-hour war, name this Central American conflict that saw rioting at subsequent sporting matches between Honduras and El Salvador.

The plan for this clash was doomed after forces for one side were crushed about a month before at La Roche-aux-Moines, which prevented their stirring up expected local revolts. In the aftermath of this battle, one of the defeated commanders was promptly restricted to his original domain of Brunswick. The aggressors counted on the support of the rebellious Ferrand of Portugal and Renaud of Dammartin, both of whom were captured in the wake of this battle, which contributed to the appointment of Frederick II as Otto IV was crushed and narrowly escaped with his freedom. The winning side was able to assert its claim to large chunks of Norman and Angevin. A decisive victory by the French over the Flemish and Germans, identify this July, 1214 battle which allowed Philip II Augustus to assert control over France and led in part to King John's granting the Magna Carta.

His first crown was allegedly taken from an effigy of the Virgin Mary. In the battle that saw his downfall, a German mercenary named Martin Schwartz was killed, and late in life, he became a royal falconer after serving loyally as a royal dishwasher. His attempt to grab power resulted in a landing at Piel Island and the battles of Bootham Bar and Doncaster, where his forces were led by John de la Pole, the Earl of Lincoln. Roger Simons educated this man and first presented him as Richard of Shrewsbury, First Duke of York, but later decided he was the Earl of Warwick. Name this man who, like Perkin Warbeck, was a pretender to the throne of Henry VII, and who lost the Battle of Stoke Field, ending the Wars of the Roses.

The winner of this battle employed a new tactic of creating an inverted wedge to trap the loser's chariots in a group of spearmen. After the eventual losers made early gains, they decided to loot instead of returning the previously captured Sisygambis. The winner of this battle broke pursuit of the loser's troops to aid his left flank, commanded by Parmenion, who was under pressure by the loser's right flank's commander Mazaeus. The winner of this battle's decisive attack split the left flank, commanded by Bessus, and the loser's central infantry. It preceded the winning commander's victory at the Hydaspes River. Name this 331 BCE battle in which Darius III saw ultimate defeat at the hands of Alexander the Great.

It was during this dynasty's reign that the "illuminationist" Ishraqi school of philosophy reached its peak under figures such as Mulla Sadra. Its last member who wielded actual power was myopically devoted to recapturing Bahrain. After that man, Shah Husayn, this dynasty continued for until the establishment of the Afsharid dynasty. Its peak was under a ruler who relied on the military advice of Sir Robert Sherley and who imported the residents of Jolfa to build his capital. The Treaty of Qasr-e Shirin ended a series of wars with its neighbor, which had defeated it at Chaldiran. Ruled by luminaries such as Tahmasp I, Abbas the Great, and Ismail I, identify this Shi'ite dynasty of Persia.

It was brought Australia by W.W. Lyght, who founded assemblies at Wagga and Syndey that came to include many members of Sydney's radical Freedom Assembly. The members of this organization took a "sacred oath" that claimed that their titular enterprise was a "philosopher's stone" that turned everything it touched into wealth, an oath called "In the beginning..." This organization, once led by James Sovereign, spearheaded successful campaigns against the Union Pacific and Wabash Railroads, and it was originally founded in secrecy under Uriah Stephens, the former head of the Garment Cutters' Association. Reaching its height under "Grand Master Workman" Terence Powderly, and losing out to the AFL after the Haymarket Square Riots, identify this first major nationwide labor organization in the United States.
the Noble Order of the Knights of Labor

During this conflict, a group of monks created a giant wooden head representing one side's leader, and kicked it around their courtyard in defiance. That side ordered the burning of the Miideri, and lost at Echizen and Tonamiyama to a commander later killed at Awazu. In the first year of this war, one side's leader was forced to hide in the Hakone mountains after losing the Battle of Ishibashiyama. Interrupted by a year-long famine, this war was sparked by a proclamation issued by Prince Mochihito at the behest of the cloistered Emperor Go-Shirakawa, and included victories at the Battles of Ichi no Tani and Yashima for Yoshitsune. Emperor Antoku drowned during this war's decisive final battle, the Battle of Dan-no-Ura. Leading to Yoritomo's creation of the Kamakura Shogunate, and recounted in The Tale of the Heike, name this 1180 to 1185 Japanese civil war between the Taira and Minamoto clans.

This man led two unsuccessful cavalry charges against the Spanish right flank at the Battle of the Dunes. His time as the High Admiral of England saw the Dutch capture over half of the British fleet in a raid on the Medway River. Archibald Campbell led a rebellion in Scotland against this ruler, who took advantage of the decision in Godden v. Hales to dispense with the Test Act when making appointments. Forces supporting this king won the Battle of Sedgemoor to end the Duke of Monmouth's Rebellion, and the English Bill of Rights attacked his abuses of power. After retreating to Ireland, he lost the Battle of the Boyne to the forces of his successor, a ruler of the House of Orange. Name this Stuart king of England, a Catholic who succeeded Charles II before being deposed by William and Mary in the Glorious Revolution.

One member of this dynasty took power after a revolution deposed William Beresford. Another member of this dynasty signed the Treaty of Badajoz to end the War of the Oranges. The Marquis of Pombal expelled the Jesuits after the Tavora conspiracy aimed to assassinate another member of this dynasty, Joseph I. Duarte Nuno pretended to be the heir of this dynasty's final king, Manuel II. One ruler from this house yelled "Independence or Death!" in a speech that came to be known as the Cry of Ipiranga. Its first ruler, known as the Restorer, was John IV, and in the 19th century, two members of this royal house became the first and second emperors of Brazil. Name this dynasty which succeeded the House of Aviz, and ruled from 1640 to 1910 in Portugal.

This gathering commissioned a revised catechism written by St. Carlo Borromeo. It defined ordination as imparting a sacramental mark on a person's soul, and its twenty-second session affirmed that the Mass was a representation, not a repetition, of Christ's sacrifice. This council fixed the number of sacraments at seven, established a distinction between fides nuda and fides caritate formata, and was reassembled by Marcellus II after being moved to Bologna. First convoked by Paul III, it appointed a commission to develop an index of prohibited books, and condemned Luther's doctrine of justification by faith. Name this ecumenical council held in three periods between 1545 and 1563, which sparked the Counter-Reformation, and took place in a city in Northern Italy.

This politician was acquitted on charges of committing adultery with the Vestal Virgin Fabia. He proposed the economic policy of tabulae novae, the cancellation of all debts, and lost his final attempt to become consul to Decimus Junius Silanus and Lucius Licinius Murena. The speech "In Toga Candida" alleged that this man cut off the head of Marcus Marius Gratidianus and carried it through the streets of Rome during the Sullan proscriptions. This politician sent Gaius Manlius to manage an army in Etruria, and met with supporters like Gaius Cornelius Cethegus and Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura at the house of Marcus Porcius Laeca. His downfall was sparked by a bundle of threatening letters discovered by Crassus. Name this man who was prosecuted by Cicero for his namesake 63 BCE conspiracy against the Roman republic.

One branch of it is notable for a tradition of writing biographies called fahrasas. The town of Ajmer is the site of the dargah of one prominent personality in this sect, Khaja Chisti, and another Indian follower of this sect is credited with the invention of the tabla and veena, Amir Khusro. The orders of this sect all invoke the silsilah as the "chain of authority" and varieties of it include the Naqshbandi, Darqawi, and Mevlevi branches. This sect, in addition to the scriptures of its parent religion, accepts also the Rishala and the Kashf of Mahjub. Members of this sect aspire to reach the state of baqa, and it is alternatively called tasawwuf because they originally only wore clothes made of wool. Though defended by the conservative al- Ghazali, its practitioners have often been persecuted for heterodoxy. Identify this sect of mystical Islam.

His translation of Shakespeare into his native language as a student inspired his initially unpopular and impractical campaign to standardize its use, while this man's final acts involved forging a key secret peace deal with members of FRODEBU. The phrase "WE HAVE PUT TOO MUCH EMPHASIS ON INDUSTRIES" appears alongside a denouncement of "gifts and loans"' and a ban on party members from holding stock in this man's attempt to explain how villagization, education, and economic nationalization would create "familyhood," or Ujammaa. The goals of that Arusha Declaration, however, faltered as his country's socialist economic program collapsed despite military victories over neighboring Uganda. Identify this African statesman who earned the title "father of the country" for uniting Tanganyika and Zanzibar and serving as the first president of Tanzania.

One siege in this war, ended by Frederic Schomberg, was supposedly marked by the heroism of a group of young boys who managed to lock the city gates as Richard Talbot's force approached Derry. A major opportunity was squandered when Tourville failed to pursue Torrington at Beachy Head, though it inspired Luxembourg to brutal efficiency at the cavalry battle of Lueze. The Prince of Waldeck also lost at Fleurus in this war, which saw land gains for the aggressors due to the ingenious siege warfare tactics of Vauban after movements by one monarch in the Palatinate led to a coalition of Spain, Savoy, England, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Netherlands opposing France's incursions. A response to the rise of Louis XIV, identify this war ended with the Treaty of Ryswick after the formation of a certain group.

In Leo Tolstoy's Resurrection, Dimitri makes a pilgrimage to one to complete his cycle of atonement. In a Jean Genet novel, Darling Daintyfoot harbors an ambition to turn Divine's room into one of these after encountering the titular Our Lady of the Flowers. A particularly hilarious moment in The Good Soldier Svejk occurs when Svejk finds Lieutenant Dub drunk in one, which causes the lieutenant to become the laughingstock of the regiment. Bonificia fulfills a destiny by joining Don Anselmo at one of these in Vargas Llosa's The Green House, while in Notes from Underground, the narrator encounters Liza after an expedition to one of these. Identify these institutions that might employ such characters as Sonya Marmeladova, Fanny Hill, or Fantine, locations at which money is often exchanged for sex.

This person rose to the position of engineer-in-chief after serving as an aide to Edwin D. Morgan in Morgan's successful run for governor. As a lawyer, he was lead counsel for the plaintiff in a case against the Third Avenue Railroad, on behalf of a woman who had been denied a seat because she was black, Elizabeth Jennings Graham. He restructured much of Buchanan's Morrill Tariff with a tariff act labeled the "Mongrel," and accepted a spot on his ticket after the refusal of Levi Morton. He gained the support of the Stalwarts, who hoped that this Roscoe Conkling protégé would champion the spoils system. Replaced on the ticket by James G. Blaine, name this president who presided over the Pendleton Act after Charles Guiteau shot James Garfield.

He authored the Bond of Association to authorize his later activities with the aid of his mentor, and his major foreign policy goal was ultimately secured in the wake of the Treaty of Joinville through the Treaty of Nonsuch. This man thwarted Thomas Morgan and Charles Paget by employing Thomas Phelippes in a then-novel capacity. An early mission to France embroiled him in the Amboise conspiracy but earned a political ally in the uncle of a man this figure would later link to a planned invasion by Henry I of Guise, Francis Throckmorton. A possible employer of Christopher Marlowe, the men who received his particular attention include ambassador Bernardino de Mendoza, banker Roberto Ridolfi, and Gilbert Gifford, whom he used to expose Anthony Babington and enact his ultimate goal of executing Mary, Queen of Scots. Identify this plot-foiling colleague of William Cecil who promoted Francis Drake and tortured his way to the top as the spymaster of Elizabeth I.

This battle occurred after one side retreated from Ford Malden, and their commanding general allegedly left the troops with Colonel Warburton while he delivered his personal luggage and family to safety. A noted battle-cry during the fighting was "Remember the Raisin!," a reference to the earlier River Raisin Massacre. One combatant in this battle was later left off the 1840 Democratic ticket, leaving Van Buren without a runningmate, and used a Vice Presidential political slogan beginning "Rumpsey Dumpsey" that referred to events in this battle; that was Richard Mentor Johnson. The battle took place near a village of Delaware Indians who had been converted to Christianity by Moravian missionaries, which is why it is called Moraviantown by the British and Canadians. Identify this October 5, 1813 skirmish in the War of 1812, the site where Tecumseh was killed.

This man abolished Oklahoma's grandfather clause in arguing Guinn v. U.S. As solicitor general, and he was the first president of the Council on Foreign Relations. He scored a major legal victory that limited the President's right to seize private property as counsel for the steel industry in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. Vs. Sawyer. He was nominated for president in a bizarre convention, during which radio listeners tuned in to hear an enthusiastic Alabama delegation yelling "UNDERWOOD!" during each round of balloting. He suffered defeat in his defense of South Carolina's educational policies in Briggs v. Elliot, a companion case to Brown v. Board of Education. He was nominated for president after a standoff between William McAdoo and Al Smith, and he ran alongside Charles W. Bryan in an election that saw Robert La Follette carry Wisconsin. Name this man who was the Democratic nominee for president in 1924 against Calvin Coolidge.

One adaptation of this collection grants large powers to rulers but implores citizens to retain their conscience. This collection's Targum caused a "great earthquake" when it was composed by Yonatan ben Uzziel, and selections from this collection are read after the Torah in the Haftara during Shabbat. Its poetic section of Acharonim contains the Trei Asar as well as the "Book of Comfort" while its narrative section of Rishonim describes the Battle of Gibea and the Judgement of Solomon. It contains books that compare Israel to a harlot, Hosea and proclaim God's love for all people, Amos. Identify this section of the Hebrew Bible consisting of many foretellings by dudes like Ezekiel and Isaiah, and which falls between the Torah and the Ketubim.

His botched funeral saw his relatives forced to pay sixty schillings for his gravesite on the spot, and may have been marred with a fire or his bowels exploding when he was shoved into his sarcophagus. His marriage to a cousin required that they donate the "Men's" and "Women's" abbeys, dedicated to St. Stephen. His loyal advisers included his half-brothers Robert and Odo, who was instrumental in putting down a revolt led by Ralph de Guader. He forced the nobles of his kingdom to swear allegiance at the Oath of Salisbury, and he faced resistance from the pretender Edgar Aetheling. He elevated the Archbishop of Canterbury over York in the Accord of Winchester, put down the Revolt of the Earls, and married Matilda of Flanders. Name this Domesday-Book-authoring, Battle-of-Hastings-winning first Norman king of England.

A schism among this entity's leaders occurred after the defeat of Henry the Younger of Brunswick-Wolfenbuttel, in which Jacob Sturm objected to a secret agreement giving the choicest parts of Brunswick-Wolfenbuttel to two of its founders. Several free cities joined this entity rather than renew the Swabian League, while cities such as Nuremberg refused to join out of mistrust for its anti-Hapsburg policies. This entity was destroyed after the capture of John Frederick of Saxony and Philip of Hesse at the Battle of Muhlberg. Name this mostly defensive alliance of Protestant German states, who were defeated in a namesake mid-sixteenth-century war by Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.

In his objections to the Treaty of Versailles, Henry Cabot Lodge compared King Hussein of the Hejaz to a king of this region. According to J. M. Letts, one of its monarchs possessed a large dog, "Carlo", and had demonstrated superiority over his people by climbing a tree that no other man could climb. The "Cleopatra Affair" involved the landing of a British force at Bluefields, the capital of this region, in violation of the Clayton-Bulwer treaty. Its last king, Henry Clarence, was deposed by Jose Zelaya during the unification of Nicaragua. Name this region bordering the Caribbean Sea, named after a native tribe and not after some pesky bloodsucking insects.

This group's followers had an early falling out over the role of the ERAP project. A meeting at Kewadin summer camp marked a shift in their membership that saw Carl Ogelsby elected their president. In the "values" section of one of its publications, it claimed that such phrases as "Capitalism Cannot Reform Itself," "All Out on May Day," and "No Cooperation with Commies and Fellow Travelers" were "incomplete." This movement spawned the RYM after its New Left Notes publication claimed "You don't need a Weatherman to know which way the wind blows." Its members elected Alan Haber as its first president, and one of its founders, Tom Hayden, was arrested as part of the Chicago Seven and wrote its Port Huron Statement. Name this radical youth movement of the 1960s that sought to incorporate like minds from universities all over the U.S.

This man attempted to debunk what he labeled "the Official Doctrine" with an analogy to a longtime village resident who is forced to draw a map of his hometown. He said that separating "the language of logic" from "the language of events" could resolve such problems as the conflict between free will and the inevitability of certain future happenings in his book Dilemmas. This author of The Thinking of Thoughts and Plato's Progress became associated with "ordinary language" philosophy after deriding what he called the "Janus-faced account of human life." From 1948 to 1971, he was the editor of the journal Mind. Name this British philosopher who attacked Cartesian dualism as "the ghost in the machine" in his book The Concept of Mind.

He created Alan Montague, the son of a Mississippi plantation owner who is present at Harper's Ferry and Fort Sumter in Manassas. The Anschluss occurs in his novel that also includes the Munich conference, Presidential Agent. That novel is part of a series revolving around the husband of the millionaire Irma, who hunts with Hermann Goering. One novel is inspired by a massacre in a mining strike in Ludlow, while Cornelia Thornwell is the central character in a novel about Sacco and Vanzetti. Jim Connor lures one of his characters into prostitution, and that woman, Ona marries a man who lives in Packingtown after emigrating from Lithuania. The creator of Lanny Budd, name this author of Boston, King Coal, Dragon's Teeth, Oil!, and a novel in which Jurgus Rudkis works in a meat packing plant, The Jungle.

The opinion in this case explained why the law in question was different from the Mann Act, the Pure Food and Drug Act, and the provisions upheld in the Lottery Case, because that law "did not regulate." This ruling stood for twenty-three years, until it was overturned in U.S. V. Darby Lumber Company. The opinion was written by William Rufus Day for the Edward White Court, which made this ruling 5-4 as McKenna, Clarke, and Brandeis joined in a dissent written by Holmes. It was brought against a U.S. Attorney in North Carolina by a man who objected to the Keating-Owen Act, which established a window of 6 A.M. To 7 P.M. And a lower age limit of fourteen. Name this 1918 ruling which ruled that Congress did not have the power to prohibit child labor.

A battle in this work is described where men strung cables into the water and wrecked their enemy's ships, while the son of one leader in this work is dissuaded from destroying the pyramids at Giza by a man who inspired the losing army to travel to the oracle of Ammon. After the Sicilian Curio's men were massacred in Libya, a meeting at Epirus is held. The survivors of the central conflict were pursued to the Hellespont, and a witch predicted the downfall of the army that included Gnaeus. At the end of this work, the sister of Cleopatra executes Ptolemy and attempts to kill a man who conquered Pharos and whose army includes the hero Scaeva and Gaius Trebonius. Name this poem in which Cato and Brutus side with Pompey, who loses the title battle to Julius Caesar, a work by Lucan.

An article by A.B. Gray described the "exceedingly beautiful and silky" cotton made available by this agreement; that article was reported on in DeBow's Review, whose editor J.D.B. DeBow was a major publicizer of this agreement's benefits. Christopher Ward advised a negotiator on one side of this agreement to settle the rejection of the Garay colonies project. The failure of this agreement's namesake to negotiate an unrelated 1832 treaty led to the Second Seminole War, during which that namesake served as quartermaster-general of the Florida Volunteers. Causes of it include the issuance of very similar grants to both Peter Hargous and A.G. Sloo, and its second article abrogated the eleventh article of an earlier treaty, which had promised costly protection from Native American raids. A bloc of northern senators held up its passage until its cost was reduced by $5 million, and its chief negotiator was formerly president of the South Carolina Railroad Company who desired to build a transcontinental railroad. Identify this 1854 agreement in which the U.S. Spent $10 million to acquire large portions of Arizona and New Mexico from Mexico.

Frostwood Elementary School is a landmark of this non-Massachusetts city's Bunker Hill Village. Bear Creek Park is located in the northwest corner of this city, whose southern suburbs include Pearland, Friendswood and Alvin. This city relies on water from Lake Conroe and its namesake lake for its daily needs, and Buffalo Bayou runs through its downtown. Its tallest building is the JPMorgan Chase Tower in this seat of Harris County. This city features the junction of Interstates 10 and 45, and other cities nearby include Katy and Galveston. It is served by George Bush Intercontinental Airport, and other landmarks in it include Reliant Stadium and Minute Maid Park. Name this largest city in Texas.

One of this battle's winning side's commanders led a unit known as the "Red Devils;" that unit gained fame for drawing this battle's first blood. The victorious general originally deployed his troops along a road known for its 69 stations, and the war surrounding this battle broke out after the splitting into factions of the Council of Five Elders. Its losing commander was beheaded at the Gamo River by a "very blunt sword." A general whose name means "small swift stream" arrived at this battle on the eventual losing side, but refused to fight, eventually defecting to the winning side after a staged volley of gunfire. That man, Kobayakawa Hideaki, thus betrayed the losing side's commanders, Ishida Mitsunari and Ankokuji Ekei. The victor, the commander of the Army of the East, still had no casus belli to kill the five-year old Toyotomi Hideyori and cement his rule, which he eventually did in the Siege of Osaka 15 years later. Identify this decisive 1600 battle in Japan which saw Tokugawa Ieyasu defeat the Toyotomi clan and gain the title of shogun.

His experience defending the Santa Fe Trail led him to improve the old muzzle-loading carbines, so in 1853, he resigned his commission to manufacture guns near Edghill, his estate. At the outbreak of the Civil War, he was appointed colonel of the First Rhode Island Regiment, and by 1862 he oversaw the First and Ninth Corps. Had his attack on the Rohrbach Bridge been more effective, the Battle of Antietam might not have been so costly. His military career ended with the Battle of the Crater, but his most famous mistake culminated in the Mud March after a failed attempt to cross the Rappahannock River. FTP, name this Civil War Union general replaced by Joseph Hooker after the Battle of Fredericksburg and known for his eponymous whiskers.

This politician argued that "the theory of our institutions guarantees to every citizen the full enjoyment of all the fruits of his industry and enterprise," but the Mills bill, which would have lowered tariffs, failed to pass. He accepted the findings in the Morgan Report concerning John Stevens's activities after being elected thanks, in part, due to publication of the "Mulligan Letters." The second term as president for this Bourbon Democrat saw the passage of the Wilson-Gorman Tariff, and he sent Nelson Miles in to break up the Pullman strike, while he had earlier passed the Interstate Commerce Act and the Dawes Act. FTP, name this president whose two terms came before and after that of Benjamin Harrison.

It only began once a Yale professor sneaked in through one of the building's windows as no one had a key to the building itself. It grew out of discussion regarding a recently passed New York Property Rights Act. James Gordon Bennett ridiculed it in the New York Herald after its second hearing, which took place in Rochester. The only measure not to be overwhelmingly approved addressed the right to vote, though it barely passed after Frederick Douglass addressed the crowd. The organizers themselves had previously met at the World's Antislavery Convention where they had been denied seats. FTP, name this 1848 New York convention organized by Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton, the first major push for women's rights.

This man fought a duel with George Finch-Hatton, in which both men aimed wide and reconciled afterwards. Earlier in his life, he had served as governor of Seringatam and Mysore, appointments made by his elder brother Richard, the then governor-general of India, and prior to that, he had served as an MP for the rotten borough of Trim in the Irish House of Commons. He married Katty Pakenham, and after his death at Walmer Castle, he would be one of the few men in his country to receive a state burial. He split witht he Tory party over a repeal of the Corn laws and retired from active politics afterwards, though he would remain Commander in Chief of the Forces until his death. Earlier in his life, this man had designed the Lines of Torres Vedras, had defeated Massena at Fuentes de Oñoro and Jourdan at Vitoria. FTP, who was this British pime minister and hero of Waterloo?

One side in this conflict fathered the so-called wagenburg tactic, an earlier version of a corral involving foot soldiers armed with crossbows and firearms taking on armored knights. The more radical faction in this conflict called for an equitable distribution of land, and advocated a departure from scholastic thought. The conflict began after the death of King Wenceslaus IV and would end with the Battle of Lipany. It included a crusade led by Emperor Sigismund in which his force was defeated at the Battle of Nemecky Brod. After the Catholic defeat, the conflict turned into civil war, as the radical Taborites, led by Prokop, lost to the moderate Utraquist faction. A faithful daughter from here had her father escape in a boat - that man Thoas, went to Tauris. This place's inhabitants were given foul body odors for not honoring Aphrodite. Visited by the Argonauts, this place is also where a certain deity hit the ground and became lame. Identify this island on which Hephaestus landed.

This man's sister Gorge slept with her own father to produce one of the seven against Thebes. According to one alternate myth, this man died when his country and the Couretes waged war, leading him to be killed at the hands of the sons of Thestios. According to another source, he was constantly pursued by the only female Argonaut, but an oracle told him to ignore her. This man fathered Polydora with his wife Cleopatra, a daughter of Marpessa. He killed his uncles Toxeus and Plexippus which lead his mother Althaia to burn a log which killed him. Name this Calydonian boar slayer.

According to Saxo-Grammaticus, the king of this name employed a powerful mace and had a penchant for terrorizing his enemies by visiting them while dressed in goat skins. That king of this name carries on a conversation with Groa and Bess. An object of this name was owned by a man who refused to trade it way for three times its weight in gold. That object's strength was tested by means of throwing wool into a river and seeing if it cleaved the wool, after it was reforged by Regin on his third try. Earlier, it had been placed into Barnstokk by Odin. Give this name for the sword of Sigurd.

Hesiod lists this man as the father of Adonis. Aelian pointed out that one figure of this name doesn't need to know arithmetic to know his own lifespan, since it is a "pupil of all wise nature." The lesser known figure of this name slept with his father's mistress Clytia at his mother Cleobule's instigation. The Metamorphoses describe how that one subsisted on a diet of frankincense. That son of Amyntor had his sight restored by Chiron and partakes in the embassy to Achilles along with Patroclus and Telamonian Ajax. The most notable figure of this name lived for six hundred years in the Arabian desert and self-immolates on its own funeral pyre. Name this legendary bird.

After winning a hard-fought battle, this hero took a bath in some springs she created while holding the skull of the defeated in one hand. Many hymns describe how this figure was born after all the gods and goddesses begged for this victor to be born. This figure rode on a mount often called Simbha and had ten hands, each of which held her weapons. A central tenet of Vaishnavism is that she slew Sumbha and Nisumbha. This figure killed the terrible buffalo demon Mahisha, and Kali could spring from her forehead when she was enraged. Name this aspect of the mother goddess Devi who was also held to be a shakti of Parvati.

In Beowulf, when Unferth is first introduced, he is said that he wants to "unbound a battle" one of these things onto Beowulf, which means he wants to challenge him. In The Saga of Grettir the Strong, Carline kills the title outlaw by using a poison made from some plant roots with these things on the individual roots. They can also be found on Arvak's Ear and Alsvith's hoof. In The Hovamol, Odin describes how he sacrificed himself to himself and found these things on a tree, which allowed him to learn deeds. One can also find them on Sleipnir's teeth and Bragi's tongue. Name these entities used in Anglo-Saxon and Scandinavian alphabets, similar to letters.

Lucian of Samosata recorded that Pan lived in a cave nearby this place so he could eavesdrop on anyone who spoke here. Anaximenes and Hyperides fought each other at this place, only for Hyperides's lover Phryne to end the quarrel by stripping naked. When the Amazons attacked Theseus, they made their base camp this raised area. The namesake of this location was a father of Alcippe that avenged her rape by killing Poseidon's son Halirrhothius. It was here where the title of semnai was bestowed by Athena to the daughters of Nyx egged on by the ghost of Clytemnestra in the last of a trilogy by Aeschylus. Name this hill in Athens associated with trials.

According to everyone's favorite mythographer Antoninus Liberalis, this man shares his name with the river where Hylas lost himself to some maidens. He is told "this is the path to the stars" by Apollo shortly before Apollo removes him from harm's way. This man's first celebrated kill was taking out Numanus, the betrothed of Juturna. Earlier, he pointed out a prophecy was true when some men "eat their tables" - this means his father's men have found Ausonia. He was succeded by Silvius in his most famous role, and this founder of Alba Longa was given an alternate name that showcased Augustus Caesar's heritage. Name this son of Aeneas.

He is taunted by a hideously ugly damsel that rides a tawny mule, carries a whip, has a beard, is a hunchback, and is going to Proud Castle. Previously, this man is reminded of his experiences when he sees three drops of geese blood on the snow. His father Gamuret committed suicide after he learned his two brothers died while in knighthood - this is why he was raised in isolation. This knight kills the Red Knight after being egged on by Sir Kay, and he finds Biaurepaire, a castle containing Blancheflor. He fails to ask a key question at a castle where he sees a bleeding lance - it belonged to the Fisher King. Name this knight whose story is told in Chretien's The Quest for the Grail.

Although he is not Endymion, this king was married to Iphianassa with whom he had Mantius, his successor. In one role, he was able to cure the daughters of Proetus and Stheneboea. In another role, he was able to help get Podarces born when he removed a knife from a tree. He then boiled it in order to make rusty water that Iphicles then drank. After being freed from Phylacus's prison, he gave his brother one third of a kingdom while he got another third of Argos. This brother of Bias also learned a secret from a pair of vultures that were devouring an ox, as well as a more immediate secret from a pair of worms in his jail cell. Name this prophet with the power to speak to animals.

Early in life, he slew Itymoneus during his war against the Eleans. One of his children mistakenly whipped Odysseus because he looked like a hobo. This father of Thrasymedes married Eurydice then had a second wife Anaxibia. He was the son of a woman who turned perfectly white, Chloris. He supposedly lived for three generations since he was given extra life by Apollo, in compensation for the death of his brothers. In The Odyssey, his son Pisistratus guides Telemachus to his court during the Telemachy. Name this hoary old king of Pylos known as the Gerenian horseman, who continuously dispenses advice.

Such as skinning] Round 02: At his death, he was put into a mound with three doors, through which peasants offered gold, silver and copper. No one speaks to this figure, nor does he eat or sleep because he did the following action: while overlooking all the worlds, he looked north and saw a beautiful lady that lifts her arms up to irradiate the sky and the sea with a sensuous light. This figure's father-in- law is married to Aurboda, and is named Gymir. Because he entrusted his sword and his horse to his servant Skirnir, he defeated the giant Beli using only an antler. He will be killed by the fire giant Surt. The owner of the folding ship Skidbladnir and the boar Gullinbursti, name this son of Skadi and Njord, a fertility god.

Ovid recorded that Arachne's father Idmon was a famous dyer of this color. A man who lost a body part of this color turned into an osprey and attacked his daughter who had just turned into an egret. Although this color is not blue, the Pindaric Odes describe the warriors who fought the harpies of King Phineus as having wings of this color. Those warriors, Zetes and Calais, are sons of Boreas, who is said to have this-colored hair. The Megaran king Nisos had a lock of it. A controversial thesis asserts that the ancient Greeks did not see the ocean as blue, but rather as this color. Identify this imperial color used in a famous dye from Tyre.

Geoffrey of Monmouth described how this guy, a sewer, perished in Arthur's battle against Lucius Tiberius, but he was useful in assisting Arthur to defeat the giant dwelling at Mont Saint-Michel. This man nicknames a certain figure "La Cote Male Taile" and has that man, Breunor le Noire fight the buffoon Dagonet. Earlier, he nicknamed Sir Gareth Beaumains. According to one of the Welsh Triads, he is one of the "Three Enchanter Knights of Britain," and he can change his height and weight to any value, not to mention he was gifted with the ability to breathe underwater for nine days. Thomas Mallory introduces us to him by having this son of Sir Ector order a servant home to retrieve a sword at a joust, only for a sword to be pulled from a stone. Name foster brother of King Arthur.
